subject: Criminology
title: 1. Basic Concepts of Crime, Criminality and Criminal Behaviour

segments.text: This is the vocabulary foundation of criminology.

Crime is legally prohibited conduct; criminality concerns propensity/patterns associated with offending; criminal behaviour studies acts and processes connected with law violation. Criminology asks not only “what happened?” but also “why, to whom, in what social setting, and how should society respond?”

Crime is a legal category: conduct becomes a crime when the applicable criminal law prohibits it and attaches criminal consequences. Criminality is broader and refers to a tendency, pattern or propensity associated with offending at the level of an individual, group or social setting. Criminal behaviour is the observable conduct that violates criminal law. Keeping these ideas separate prevents circular explanations such as “he offended because he is criminal.”

Criminology studies why offences occur, how crime is distributed, how institutions respond and how prevention can work. Legal guilt, by contrast, is decided through criminal procedure and evidence. A criminological explanation can help us understand risk without deciding whether a particular person is legally guilty.

blocks.text: Crime as a changing social and legal category

segments.text: What counts as crime changes across time and jurisdictions because legislatures amend prohibitions, social harms become newly recognized and enforcement priorities shift. Some acts may be socially condemned without being criminal, while technical offences may carry legal punishment even where public moral condemnation is weak.

This makes definition important. Researchers must specify whether they are measuring police-recorded offences, victimization, self-reported offending, convictions or another indicator. Each measure captures a different part of the phenomenon.

Criminal behaviour rarely has one universal cause. Research examines interacting factors at individual, family, peer, neighbourhood, economic and institutional levels. A risk factor increases the likelihood of an outcome in a population; it does not prove that every exposed person will offend.

A useful causal map is: background conditions → opportunities and pressures → individual interpretation and social learning → decision or behaviour → institutional response → possible reinforcement or desistance. Different theories emphasize different links in this chain.

Criminology goes beyond asking whether a legal offence occurred. It also asks who offends, who is victimized, what social and individual factors are associated with offending, how institutions respond and which prevention strategies work.
individual factors such as personality or development; group or community factors such as peers and neighbourhood; and structural factors such as inequality, institutions or social change.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not use “crime,” “criminality” and “criminal behaviour” as interchangeable terms. Each describes a different level of analysis.
